title: Semiconductors
description: Band gaps, doping, and the electronics revolution

concepts.title: Conductors, Insulators, Semiconductors
concepts.contentHtml:
Solids are classified electronically by their band structure:

  • Metals — partially filled conduction band; electrons are free at any temperature. Resistivity ~10⁻⁸ Ω·m.
  • Insulators — wide band gap (E_g > 3 eV). At room temperature essentially no electrons reach the conduction band. Resistivity ~10¹⁶ Ω·m.
  • Semiconductors — narrow band gap (typically 0.5–3 eV). At T = 0 K they would be insulators, but at room temperature thermal excitation lifts a small but useful number of electrons across the gap.

Common semiconductors: silicon (1.12 eV), germanium (0.66 eV), gallium arsenide (1.42 eV), gallium nitride (3.4 eV), silicon carbide (3.0 eV).

Semiconductors are interesting precisely because their conductivity sits between extremes — and can be tuned across many orders of magnitude by doping, temperature, light, and electric field. That tunability is what makes electronics possible.

concepts.title: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic
concepts.contentHtml:
Intrinsic semiconductors are pure: every conduction electron leaves a hole behind. Their conductivity rises exponentially with temperature.

Extrinsic semiconductors are deliberately doped:

  • n-type — donors (P, As in Si) provide extra electrons.
  • p-type — acceptors (B, Al in Si) provide extra holes.

One dopant atom per million silicon atoms can change conductivity by orders of magnitude. The semiconductor industry routinely controls doping to better than parts per billion. The Fermi level — the chemical potential of electrons — sits near mid-gap in intrinsic material, near the conduction band in n-type, and near the valence band in p-type.

Joining n-type to p-type produces a p-n junction: the basis of every diode, transistor, LED, and solar cell.

concepts.title: Beyond Silicon
concepts.contentHtml:
Silicon dominates digital electronics, but other semiconductors fill specialised roles:

  • GaAs, InGaAs, InP — high-speed RF devices, laser diodes, multi-junction solar cells. Direct band gap suits emission and absorption.
  • GaN, SiC — wide-band-gap (WBG) power electronics. They handle higher voltages, higher temperatures, and switch faster than silicon. Found in modern fast chargers, EV inverters, and power grids.
  • InGaN, AlInGaP — visible-spectrum LEDs (blue, green, red). The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics rewarded the development of efficient blue InGaN LEDs that enabled white LED lighting.
  • CdTe, CIGS — thin-film solar cells. Direct band gap allows efficient absorption in 1–2 µm of material.
  • Organic semiconductors — flexible OLEDs, printed transistors, photovoltaics.
  • Halide perovskites — fast-rising in solar and LEDs.

The right semiconductor for a job depends on the band gap, mobility, manufacturing scale, and target wavelength.

title: Magnetic Materials
description: Domains, hysteresis, and the difference between hard and soft magnets

concepts.title: Origins of Magnetism in Solids
concepts.contentHtml:
Atomic-scale magnetism comes from electron spin and orbital angular momentum. In a solid, the collective behaviour determines macroscopic magnetic response:

  • Diamagnetic — all materials weakly repel a field; usually negligible.
  • Paramagnetic — unpaired spins align weakly with applied field.
  • Ferromagnetic — spins align parallel to each other below the Curie temperature, even with no applied field. Iron, cobalt, nickel, and many alloys.
  • Antiferromagnetic — adjacent spins align opposite, cancelling out (e.g. NiO).
  • Ferrimagnetic — opposite alignment with unequal magnitudes, leaving net magnetisation. Includes magnetite (Fe₃O₄) and most ferrites used in transformer cores.

The transition from ordered to disordered spin configurations at the Curie (ferromagnet) or Néel (antiferromagnet) temperature is a continuous phase transition with magnetisation as the order parameter.

concepts.title: Magnetic Domains and Hysteresis
concepts.contentHtml:
A bulk ferromagnet does not appear magnetised in its 'natural' state because it splits into domains: regions in which all spins are aligned, but with different orientations between domains, cancelling overall.

Applying an external field grows the domains aligned with the field at the expense of others. As the field is reversed and removed, the response is non-linear and irreversible — the famous hysteresis loop:

  • Saturation magnetisation M_s — the limit when all spins align.
  • Remanence M_r — what remains after the field is removed.
  • Coercivity H_c — the reverse field needed to bring magnetisation back to zero.

Hysteresis loop area equals the energy dissipated per cycle — relevant for AC magnetic applications.

concepts.title: Soft vs Hard Magnets
concepts.contentHtml:
Engineering magnets fall into two categories:

  • Soft magnets — narrow hysteresis loop, low coercivity (< 1 kA/m). Used in transformers, motor laminations, electromagnets. Examples: silicon steel (Fe-Si), permalloy (Ni-Fe), amorphous metallic glasses, soft ferrites. The goal is high permeability and low loss per cycle.
  • Hard magnets — wide hysteresis loop, high coercivity (> 100 kA/m), high remanence. Used as permanent magnets. Examples: ferrite (BaFe₁₂O₁₉, SrFe₁₂O₁₉), alnico (Al-Ni-Co-Fe), samarium-cobalt (SmCo₅), neodymium-iron-boron (Nd₂Fe₁₄B — the strongest commercial permanent magnet).

Nd-Fe-B magnets revolutionised wind turbines, electric vehicles, and consumer electronics by combining extreme strength with manageable mass. Their dependence on rare-earth elements makes their supply chain a current strategic concern.

title: Piezoelectrics and Ferroelectrics
description: Materials that generate voltage from squeeze — and remember it

concepts.title: The Piezoelectric Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
The piezoelectric effect, discovered by the Curie brothers in 1880, is the production of an electric voltage in a crystal in response to mechanical stress — and the reciprocal: mechanical strain in response to an applied voltage.

Piezoelectricity requires a non-centrosymmetric crystal structure. Among the 32 crystal classes, 21 are non-centrosymmetric, and 20 of those are piezoelectric. Common examples: quartz (SiO₂), Rochelle salt, lithium niobate (LiNbO₃), zinc oxide (ZnO), the polymer PVDF, and especially lead-zirconate-titanate (PZT, Pb(Zr,Ti)O₃).

Applications:

  • Quartz oscillators in every digital clock and microcontroller.
  • Ultrasound transducers in medical imaging and industrial NDT.
  • Inkjet printer nozzles, fuel injectors, atomic-force microscope scanners.
  • Buzzer elements, lighters, sonar.

concepts.title: Ferroelectricity
concepts.contentHtml:
A subset of piezoelectric materials are ferroelectric: they have a spontaneous electric polarisation that can be reversed by an external field. The polarisation–field response shows a hysteresis loop directly analogous to ferromagnets.

The classic ferroelectric is barium titanate (BaTiO₃), a perovskite with a small Ti⁴⁺ ion that can sit on either side of the centre of its TiO₆ octahedron, producing a non-zero dipole. Cooling through the Curie temperature (~120 °C) breaks the centrosymmetry, and the crystal develops permanent polarisation.

PZT (lead zirconate titanate) is the workhorse industrial ferroelectric/piezoelectric. Recent regulatory pressure to remove lead is driving research on lead-free alternatives based on (K,Na)NbO₃ and similar perovskites.

concepts.title: Pyroelectric and Multiferroic Materials
concepts.contentHtml:
Two more functional cousins:

  • Pyroelectric — temperature changes produce a voltage. Used in passive infrared (PIR) motion detectors and thermal imaging arrays.
  • Multiferroic — exhibits more than one 'ferroic' order at once (ferroelectric + ferromagnetic, for instance). BiFeO₃ is the most studied. Multiferroics could enable electric writing of magnetic memory bits — exciting for future low-power data storage.

The hierarchy is: every ferroelectric is piezoelectric and pyroelectric, but not every piezoelectric is ferroelectric. Quartz is piezoelectric without being ferroelectric. PZT and BaTiO₃ are all three. Multiferroics add a magnetic order on top.

This whole family rests on broken symmetry: each functional property requires the absence of a particular symmetry element in the crystal. Materials engineering at this level is essentially symmetry engineering.

title: Superconductors
description: Zero resistance — and the materials that achieve it

concepts.title: The Superconducting State
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1911 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled mercury below 4.2 K and discovered its electrical resistance dropped to zero. The phenomenon is superconductivity:

  • Zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature T_c.
  • Expulsion of magnetic field lines from the bulk (the Meissner effect, 1933) — superconductors are perfect diamagnets, not just perfect conductors.
  • A finite critical magnetic field H_c above which superconductivity is destroyed.
  • A finite critical current density J_c above which it is also destroyed.

Below T_c, electrons pair up into Cooper pairs mediated by lattice vibrations (phonons) — explained by Bardeen, Cooper, and Schrieffer in 1957 (BCS theory, Nobel 1972). The pairs flow without scattering because the energy gap forbids ordinary single-electron scattering processes.

concepts.title: Type I, Type II, and the Critical Field
concepts.contentHtml:
Two classes of superconductors, distinguished by their response to magnetic field:

  • Type I — completely expels field below H_c, then abruptly reverts to normal. Most pure metallic elements (Pb, Hg, Sn).
  • Type II — has two critical fields. Below H_c1 the material fully superconducts; between H_c1 and H_c2 magnetic flux penetrates as quantised flux tubes (Abrikosov vortices), but supercurrents continue around them. Above H_c2 the material is normal. All practical superconducting magnets are Type II.

The world's strongest electromagnets — for MRI scanners, particle accelerators, and ITER tokamak — use Type II niobium-titanium (NbTi, T_c = 9.2 K) or niobium-tin (Nb₃Sn, T_c = 18 K), cooled with liquid helium to ~4 K.

concepts.title: High-T_c, Iron-Based, and Hydride Superconductors
concepts.contentHtml:
For 75 years T_c crept upward from 4 K to ~23 K. In 1986 Bednorz and Müller discovered cuprate superconductors based on copper oxide planes (La₂CuO₄, then YBa₂Cu₃O₇ at 93 K, exceeding the boiling point of liquid nitrogen at 77 K). The Nobel Prize followed in 1987.

Cuprates remain the highest-T_c materials at ambient pressure (HgBaCaCuO at ~135 K), but they are brittle ceramics — extraordinarily challenging to wind into magnets. They are nevertheless used in fault-current limiters and a generation of high-field accelerator magnets.

In the 2010s, hydrogen-rich superconductors at extreme pressure pushed T_c even higher: H₃S at ~203 K and 150 GPa (2015), LaH₁₀ at ~250 K and 170 GPa (2019). These are not yet practical materials — the pressures are unattainable in any everyday device — but they demonstrate that conventional phonon-mediated superconductivity can survive almost to room temperature.

Room-temperature superconductivity at ambient pressure remains one of the great open prizes of materials science.

title: Frontiers — Metamaterials and Multifunctional
description: Designing matter for properties nature does not provide

concepts.title: Metamaterials
concepts.contentHtml:
Metamaterials are engineered structures whose properties are dominated by their geometric design rather than their bulk chemistry. By patterning a material with sub-wavelength features (~λ/10), one can create:

  • Negative-index materials — bend light backwards, demonstrated experimentally by Smith et al. (2000). Forms the basis of cloaking and superlens proposals.
  • Acoustic metamaterials — block, focus, or steer sound at sub-wavelength scales.
  • Mechanical metamaterials — exhibit negative Poisson's ratio (auxetic materials get fatter when stretched), zero compressibility, or programmable load-deformation curves.
  • Photonic crystals — periodic dielectric structures with optical band gaps; the basis of low-loss fibre lasers, structural colours in butterflies, and engineered light extraction in LEDs.

Metamaterials separate properties from chemistry: the same plain steel becomes auxetic if you punch the right pattern of holes, and the same air becomes opaque to certain frequencies if you arrange resonators in the right lattice.

concepts.title: Multifunctional and Smart Materials
concepts.contentHtml:
A multifunctional material performs more than one job simultaneously — load-bearing while sensing, conducting while harvesting energy, structural while self-healing.

Examples:

  • Carbon-fibre composites with embedded piezoelectric layers — monitor their own structural health, providing real-time strain or damage data without external sensors.
  • Self-healing polymers — microcapsules of monomer rupture in cracks and polymerise to seal them. Vehicle paints, insulation, and aerospace coatings now use this approach.
  • Phase-change materials — store thermal energy by repeatedly melting and re-freezing (paraffins, salt hydrates). Used in passive building cooling and thermal management of electronics.
  • Photovoltaic-thermoelectric hybrids — convert both light (PV) and the resulting heat (TE) into useful energy.

Multifunctionality moves the design problem up a level: not 'what alloy do we use' but 'what combination of phases, structures, and properties does this part need to deliver simultaneously?'

concepts.title: Biomaterials and Bio-Inspired Design
concepts.contentHtml:
Living systems are masters of multifunctional materials assembled at room temperature from cheap ingredients:

  • Bone — hydroxyapatite reinforced with collagen, hierarchically structured from the molecular to the macroscopic. Strong, tough, lightweight, and self-repairing.
  • Nacre (mother of pearl) — 95 % aragonite (CaCO₃) plus 5 % protein, with brick-and-mortar microstructure giving toughness 1000× that of pure aragonite.
  • Spider silk — combines extreme strength and toughness in a self-assembled protein fibre.
  • Adhesion in geckos — vast arrays of nanoscale hairs producing van der Waals adhesion without glue.

Bio-inspired engineering tries to copy these strategies — hierarchical structuring, brick-and-mortar layouts, designed defects, self-assembly from solution — to make tougher ceramics, lighter composites, and reusable adhesives.

The implicit lesson is that performance often comes not from which atoms are used but from how they are organised across length scales. That is the modern programme of materials science: writing the recipe for matter, not just discovering what already exists.
